title: Monsters Martians and Paranormal Megabucks - Marketplace Special 26
excerpt: As networks weaponise prestige IP and dystopian visions of the future, television’s horror, sci-fi and supernatural programming is undergoing a major industrial and creative recalibration. Driven by soaring production budgets and fierce streaming competition, this genre has abandoned campy, episodic formulas in favour of high-concept, character-driven psychological dramas. This season dissects the market forces driving this shift, how studios are leveraging cinematic franchises and what new titles are emerging from the shadows.
content:
Campaign Profile

Scares and sci-fi find new routes to screen as premieres shrink

24-11-2026

As research shows fewer horror, sci-fi and supernatural series reaching screens, a mix of franchise extensions, licensed hits and independent originals is shaping what arrives next.

Netflix’s decision to commission a live-action prequel to Stranger Things, announced earlier this month, is the highest-profile new genre project in development, but it lands at a time when the number of horror, sci-fi and supernatural series reaching screens is shrinking. Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure, set in 1950s Nevada, reunites the Duffer Brothers with showrunner Kate Trefry, with Joe Wright (Pride & Prejudice, Atonement, Darkest Hour) directing.

Despite this major sci-fi greenlight, data from Parrot Analytics shows the genre made up 2.3% of new series premieres in 2020 but 1.8% by October 2026, while its share of global series demand fell from 8.4% to 5.4% over the same period. Netflix’s genre premieres dropped from more than 30 in 2022 to nine in 2025, and Amazon’s from 14 in 2023 to six in 2025. Christofer Hamilton, industry insights manager at Parrot, links the decline to budget pressure. “If you’re looking to trim budgets, these are going to be the big pricey titles,” he says.

The titles that do get made often carry established IP. The highest-demand genre premieres of 2025 were Disney+ series Daredevil: Born Again, HBO Max’s It: Welcome to Derry and FX’s Alien: Earth, while MGM+’s Spider-Noir and Disney+ title Wonder Man are among the highest-demand premieres of 2026 so far. Other Worlds fits that pattern, though with an entirely new cast it is likely to cost less than the series that inspired it, whose budget reportedly ballooned over a nine-year run.

Elsewhere, buyers are pursuing different routes. At MGM+, horror mystery From is the service’s best-performing show ever. After being licensed to Netflix, it launched there on October 19 and was the number one streaming programme in the US for two weeks in a row, according to Nielsen. The fifth and final season has begun production for release in 2027. “If you are in my line of work, you pray for a show like From that is just so successful,” says Michael Wright, global head of MGM+.

MGM+ is looking to build on that success. A second season of The Institute, based on Stephen King’s 2019 novel, is airing, and the service has greenlit The Black Tapes, an eight-part adaptation of the 2015 podcast of the same name, which amassed 60 million downloads. Created by Terry Miles and Paul Bae, it stars Nikolaj Coster-Waldau as Dr Richard Strand and goes into production in Vancouver in January.

Wright says two further high-profile science fiction series are in the works, one of which he expects will “almost certainly” be greenlit within the next several months. He says the wider decline does not apply to his service. “I guess we’re zigging while Parrot Analytics is zagging because horror genre has worked very well for us over the last couple of years,” he says.

Shudder, owned by IFC Entertainment Group, is taking a different approach, using cinema releases to feed its streaming service. Breeder was released theatrically on October 28 and arrives on Shudder in January, following the same path as Whistle, This Is Not a Test, Dolly and Forbidden Fruits, each of which had a theatrical window this year.

The model’s reference point is Good Boy, which reportedly cost US$70,000 to make and grossed approximately US$6m at the domestic box office and US$8.8m worldwide before moving to streaming. “The theatrical release for many films can be a very strong advertising campaign for its streaming life,” notes IFC Entertainment Group head Scott Shooman.

Shudder’s scripted series output has been scaling back for several years, but Shooman points to the completed third season of The Creep Tapes, and a sequel to In a Violent Nature is due in February. He says franchise IP matters less to a filmmaker-led model, yet he does not rule it out. “Original is original and unique is unique, and that’s also noisy. We like both ends of that spectrum, and if they overlap, even better,” he says.

Original creator voices are also the pitch at Pacesetter Productions, which is producing season eight of Black Mirror for delivery next year. Its most recent genre release, Below, marked the most-viewed debut of a Netflix Canadian title, reaching number one on the Global Top 10 English TV list with 17 million views and ranking number one in 53 countries, according to Netflix’s own performance data.

The company is also in production on Blackmere, a British dark crime-comedy created by Charlie Brooker for Netflix, which is scheduled to premiere in 2027 and stars Paddy Considine, Georgina Campbell, Lena Headey and Rory Kinnear. Founder and CEO Jessica Rhoades says her development focus is moving towards regional production. “I’m really a fan of regional production. I really believe in it. I’ve become a full believer that small is big,” she says.

New entrants are testing the space too. US feature producer K Period Media, founded by Kimberly Steward in 2013 and known for Suspiria and Manchester by the Sea, is finishing Recap, its first original, independently financed television series. The high-concept psychological and mystery thriller with elements of horror stars Corey Stoll and Julia Stiles, and was developed with remarkable speed: the writers room launched in May 2025, production began in October 2025 and filming wrapped in March 2026. Distributed by Fifth Season, it has already been acquired by a streaming platform for the US and a number of international territories, according to chief operating officer Alex Foster.

“We are new to the TV space and definitely new to the international TV space,” Foster tells C21. He says the show has persuaded the company to commit to the medium. “There is a model here to make independent television that can be really premium and really satisfying and land with audiences. With Recap, we prove that model, and so now TV becomes a major part of our business for sure,” he says.

Audience appetite is not the constraint. Ampere Analysis’s Q3 2026 consumer survey found horror was US consumers’ most-named favourite genre for the first time, cited by 11.4%, and US SVoD platforms offered a record 5,462 hours of horror movie content in the quarter. The projects now reaching the market suggest the genre is being reshaped rather than abandoned, with franchise extensions at the top end, licensed hits and theatrical-first films in the middle, and smaller independent originals testing what can be made for less.
